lesson:
# Loop pipelining: latency and throughput

Loop pipelining overlaps successive iterations of a loop so that a new one starts every II cycles. It is the single most effective HLS transformation for loops, because it raises throughput by up to the iteration latency divided by II, often at modest area cost. Its cost model, total cycles, iterations in flight and speedup, is simple and should be computed by reflex.

## Total cycles of a pipelined loop

With $N$ iterations, an initiation interval II and an iteration latency $L$, the last iteration starts $(N - 1)\,\mathrm{II}$ cycles after the first and takes $L$ cycles, so the loop takes $(N - 1)\,\mathrm{II} + L$ cycles. A loop of 423 iterations with II = 1 and $L = 22$ takes $422 + 22 = 444$ cycles, against $423 \times 22 = 9306$ unpipelined. For long loops the $(N - 1)\,\mathrm{II}$ term dominates, so II, not latency, decides performance. The formula assumes no stalls; variable-latency memory or stream back-pressure stretches it, and HLS reports then give a minimum and a maximum. A loop nested inside an outer loop pays the fill and drain of $L - \mathrm{II}$ cycles on every outer iteration unless the loops are flattened or the outer loop is pipelined too.

## Iterations in flight and pipeline depth

Each iteration lives for $L$ cycles and a new one starts every II cycles, so at most $\lceil L / \mathrm{II} \rceil$ iterations are in flight at once. This is the pipeline's stage count, the number of stages of II cycles that one iteration's schedule is cut into. With II = 1 and $L = 5$, five iterations overlap; with II = 4 and $L = 12$, three do. Every in-flight iteration needs its own copy of each value that is live across stage boundaries, so register count grows with depth: a value live for 6 cycles in a pipeline at II = 1 needs 6 registers, one per overlapping iteration. That is the area price of pipelining, together with the extra units needed to sustain the II, and it is why a deeply pipelined loop at II = 1 can be much larger than its unpipelined version.

## Speedup and its limit

The speedup over running iterations back to back is $\frac{N L}{(N - 1)\,\mathrm{II} + L}$. For 182 iterations with $L = 12$ and II = 4 it is $2184 / 736 = 2.97$. As $N$ grows, it approaches $L / \mathrm{II}$, here 3; for short loops the fill and drain eat into it, and a loop of 2 iterations gains almost nothing. This limit tells a designer what pipelining can buy before running the tool, and how to get more: reduce II, by adding resources, partitioning memories or breaking recurrences, or reduce the work per iteration. It also shows why a modest II on a long loop often beats aggressive unrolling: unrolling multiplies area by the unroll factor, while pipelining at II = 1 reuses one copy of the body.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Loop unrolling and its trade-offs

Unrolling replicates a loop body U times and runs the loop N/U times, exposing operations from several iterations in one larger basic block. It creates spatial parallelism, at the price of area and memory bandwidth, and it interacts with every other knob: resource limits, memory ports, recurrences and pipelining. Knowing where unrolling stops paying is the core of HLS design-space intuition.

## Main loop and remainder

Unrolling by U turns $N$ iterations into $\lfloor N / U \rfloor$ trips of a U-wide body. If the compiler cannot prove $N$ is a multiple of U, it must also handle the leftover $N \bmod U$ iterations, either with a separate remainder loop or by guarding each copy of the body with a condition. A loop of 105 iterations unrolled by 4 runs 26 main trips covering 104 iterations and one remainder iteration. Guards cost little but prevent some optimizations; a remainder loop costs extra control states. Full unrolling, U = N, removes the loop entirely and is only possible with a constant trip count. Partial unrolling exposes U iterations' operations to the scheduler at once, so independent iterations can execute in parallel, but only if units and memory ports exist to serve them.

## Cycles under resource limits

Model each unrolled body as taking the larger of its dependence depth $D$ and its resource bounds. With $a$ multiplications and $b$ additions per iteration, $k_m$ multipliers and $k_a$ adders, and independent iterations, one body of U copies takes $\max(D, \lceil U a / k_m \rceil, \lceil U b / k_a \rceil)$ cycles, and the loop takes that times $N / U$. With $a = 2$, $b = 3$, $D = 5$, three multipliers, three adders and U = 4, the body takes $\max(5, 3, 4) = 5$ cycles, and 32 iterations take $8 \times 5 = 40$ cycles, against 160 without unrolling. Unrolling helps exactly while the depth term dominates, because the extra copies then run in the shadow of the dependence chain. This model ignores pipelining across trips, which is usually combined with unrolling in practice.

## Where unrolling stops paying

The body stays at $D$ cycles while $\lceil U a / k_m \rceil \le D$ and $\lceil U b / k_a \rceil \le D$, that is for $U \le \min(\lfloor D k_m / a \rfloor, \lfloor D k_a / b \rfloor)$. With $D = 5$, one multiplier and $a = 2$, the multiplier allows $U \le 2$; beyond that, each extra copy adds cycles in proportion and the loop time stops falling, while area and multiplexers keep growing. The same reasoning applies to memory: U reads per trip from an array with $p$ ports cost $\lceil U / p \rceil$ cycles, so unrolling without array partitioning is often wasted. Recurrences limit unrolling too: unrolling a loop with an accumulator only lengthens the dependence chain through the accumulator unless it is reassociated. The right factor is the largest one the binding constraint can absorb, not the largest the area budget allows.

## Going deeper

# The resource-constrained minimum II

ResMII is the lowest II that the available resources allow, whatever the dependences. In every window of II cycles, each resource must serve all of one iteration's uses of it. It is one of the two lower bounds every modulo scheduler computes first, and it explains most II violations an HLS report shows, especially those caused by memory ports.

## One resource type

In steady state a pipelined loop starts one iteration every II cycles, so every II cycles each resource must perform one iteration's worth of work. If an iteration uses resource $r$ for $u_r$ cycles in total and there are $k_r$ copies, then $k_r \cdot \mathrm{II} \ge u_r$, so $\mathrm{II} \ge \lceil u_r / k_r \rceil$. Ten multiplications per iteration on four fully pipelined multipliers give $\lceil 10 / 4 \rceil = 3$: at II = 2 the multipliers would offer only 8 slots for 10 uses. For a non-pipelined unit each use occupies it for its whole latency, so $u_r$ is the number of uses times the occupancy. The bound depends only on counts, so it is computed before scheduling and costs nothing.

## ResMII over all resources

Every resource gives its own bound, and ResMII is the maximum: $\mathrm{ResMII} = \max_r \lceil u_r / k_r \rceil$. With 6 multiplications on 4 multipliers, 2 additions on 4 adders and 1 division on 1 divider, the bounds are 2, 1 and 1, so ResMII = 2. The resource with the largest bound is the binding resource; adding copies of any other resource does nothing for the II. That is why HLS reports name the limiting resource. The bound can be loose when uses of different resources must line up in particular cycles, and modulo scheduling may then need a larger II, but in practice ResMII is usually achieved when it dominates. Reducing it means more copies of the binding resource, or fewer uses through algebraic rewriting or operator sharing across iterations.

## Memory ports as resources

Memories are the most common binding resource. A block RAM has one or two ports, each performing one read or one write per cycle. An iteration that reads array A six times and writes it twice makes 8 accesses; in a single-port RAM that forces $\mathrm{II} \ge 8$, in a dual-port RAM $\mathrm{II} \ge 4$. If the same iteration needs only $\lceil 8 / 2 \rceil = 4$ cycles of multiplier time, memory is still the binding resource. The remedies are array partitioning, which splits A into banks with their own ports, reshaping, which packs several elements into one wide word, and restructuring the code so that values are read once and reused from registers. A report saying the II is limited by a memory port is therefore a request to change the memory architecture, not the arithmetic.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# The recurrence-constrained minimum II

RecMII is the lowest II that a loop's dependence cycles allow, however many resources are available. A value computed in one iteration and needed by a later one forms a cycle in the loop's dependence graph, and the operations on that cycle must complete within the time the iteration distance allows. Recurrences are why some loops refuse to reach II = 1 no matter how much hardware is added.

## One recurrence

Give every dependence edge $u \to v$ a latency $l_u$ and an iteration distance $d$, the number of iterations it spans: 0 within an iteration, 1 from one iteration to the next. In a modulo schedule the edge requires $s_v + d\,\mathrm{II} \ge s_u + l_u$. Summing around a cycle $C$, the start times cancel and leave $\mathrm{II} \cdot \sum_C d \ge \sum_C l$. So each cycle gives $\mathrm{II} \ge \lceil \sum l / \sum d \rceil$. An accumulation whose cycle holds a 12-cycle floating-point adder and has distance 1 needs $\mathrm{II} \ge 12$: iteration $i + 1$ cannot start its addition until iteration $i$'s result exists. With distance 2, as when each iteration updates a value used two iterations later, the bound halves to 6.

## RecMII over all cycles

A loop may have several elementary cycles, and RecMII is the maximum of their bounds. With cycles of latency 4 and distance 2, latency 7 and distance 3, latency 17 and distance 3, and latency 14 and distance 3, the bounds are 2, 3, 6 and 5, so RecMII = 6. Computing it exactly does not require enumerating cycles, which can be exponential in number. Instead, a tool tests a candidate II by checking whether the graph with edge weights $l_u - d\,\mathrm{II}$ has a positive cycle, using a longest-path or Floyd-Warshall pass, and searches for the smallest II without one. That is the same positive-cycle test that decides feasibility of an SDC system, applied to the modulo constraints. The minimum II is then $\max(\mathrm{ResMII}, \mathrm{RecMII})$.

## Reading cycles from a loop body

In a loop body written as a chain of dependent operations $o_1 \to o_2 \to \dots \to o_n$, a loop-carried edge from $o_j$ back to $o_i$, with $i \le j$, closes a cycle through $o_i, \dots, o_j$. Its latency is the sum of those operations' latencies, and its distance is the edge's distance. With latencies 1, 2, 3, 4 and 4, an edge $o_5 \to o_1$ of distance 2 gives $\lceil 14 / 2 \rceil = 7$, and a self-edge $o_3 \to o_3$ of distance 2 gives $\lceil 3 / 2 \rceil = 2$, so RecMII = 7. Memory dependences count too: a store to $a[i]$ followed by a load of $a[i-1]$ in the next iteration is a carried edge of distance 1 through memory, and if the tool cannot prove the addresses differ, it must assume such an edge, which can make RecMII large.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Modulo scheduling

Modulo scheduling builds one schedule for a single iteration such that the same schedule, started every II cycles, never overuses a resource or violates a dependence. It is how HLS tools pipeline loops, inherited from software pipelining for VLIW processors. The key structure is the modulo reservation table, which folds time modulo II so that resource conflicts between overlapping iterations become conflicts in one table.

## The modulo reservation table

When iterations start every II cycles, an operation scheduled at time $t$ of its iteration executes at $t$, $t + \mathrm{II}$, $t + 2\,\mathrm{II}$ and so on in absolute time, once per iteration. In steady state, all operations whose times share the same residue $t \bmod \mathrm{II}$ execute in the same cycle, from different iterations. The modulo reservation table has II rows, and each operation reserves its resource in row $t \bmod \mathrm{II}$. A schedule is resource-legal when no row of the table uses more copies of a resource than exist. With II = 5 and multiplications at times 8, 9, 9, 10 and 12, the rows are 3, 4, 4, 0 and 2, so row 4 holds two multiplications and the schedule needs two multipliers, or one multiplication must move.

## Iterative modulo scheduling

Rau's iterative modulo scheduling starts with $\mathrm{II} = \max(\mathrm{ResMII}, \mathrm{RecMII})$. It schedules operations in priority order. For each one it computes the earliest start allowed by already-scheduled predecessors, including carried edges through the term $-d\,\mathrm{II}$, and then tries times $t, t + 1, \dots, t + \mathrm{II} - 1$ until it finds a free row in the table; trying more than II consecutive times is pointless, because the rows repeat. With II = 5, one multiplier, rows 0 occupied and an earliest start of 10, time 10 falls in row 0 and is blocked, and time 11 falls in free row 1, so the operation starts at 11. If no row is free, the algorithm evicts a conflicting operation and reschedules it later, within a budget; if the budget runs out, it increases II and starts again.

## Stages, prologue and epilogue

The finished schedule of one iteration has some length $SL$; cutting it into blocks of II cycles gives $S = \lceil SL / \mathrm{II} \rceil$ stages. In the steady-state kernel, stage $k$ of iteration $i$ runs alongside stage $k - 1$ of iteration $i + 1$, and so on, so all $S$ stages are busy. Before that, a prologue of $(S - 1)\,\mathrm{II}$ cycles fills the pipeline one stage at a time, and after the last iteration starts, an epilogue of the same length drains it. With II = 3 and $SL = 10$, there are 4 stages, and the prologue lasts 9 cycles. In HLS the prologue and epilogue are usually realized with stage-valid bits rather than separate code. Short loops spend a large fraction of their time in fill and drain, which is why tools offer to flatten nested loops into one long pipelined loop.

lesson:
# Breaking recurrences with partial sums

When RecMII is the binding bound, more hardware cannot help: the loop must be rewritten so that its dependence cycle is shorter or spans more iterations. The classic case is a floating-point accumulation whose adder latency sets the II. Interleaved partial sums, a form of reassociation, raise the iteration distance of the recurrence and recover II = 1, at the cost of a final reduction and changed rounding.

## What sits on the recurrence

Identify which operations lie on the loop-carried cycle. In $s = s + x[i]$, only the addition is on it, so with a pipelined adder of latency $L_a$ and distance 1, $\mathrm{RecMII} = L_a$. In $s = s + a[i] \times b[i]$, the multiplication reads only array values and is off the cycle; it can be computed ahead in the pipeline, so RecMII is still $L_a$. In $s = s \times c + x[i]$, both the multiplication and the addition are on the cycle, so $\mathrm{RecMII} = L_m + L_a$: with a 6-cycle multiplier and a 5-cycle adder, II = 11. Moving every operation that does not depend on the carried value off the cycle is the first step of any recurrence fix, and HLS tools do much of it automatically during scheduling.

## Interleaved partial sums

Keep $P$ partial sums and let iteration $i$ update partial sum $i \bmod P$. Each partial sum is now updated every $P$ iterations, so its recurrence has distance $P$, and the bound becomes $\lceil L_a / P \rceil$. To reach a target II, choose $P \ge \lceil L_a / \mathrm{II} \rceil$: an 8-cycle adder reaches II = 3 with $P = 3$, and II = 1 with $P = 8$. The rewrite is a reassociation of the sum. On integers it is exact. On floating point it changes the order of additions and therefore the rounding, so tools do it only when the user permits, and the verification must use a tolerance. Unrolling an accumulation without this rewrite does not help: the unrolled body still has a single chain through $s$, now even longer.

## Total cost including the final reduction

After the loop, the $P$ partial sums must be combined. A balanced tree takes $\lceil \log_2 P \rceil$ levels of additions, each costing $L_a$ cycles. With $N$ values, the main loop at II = 1 issues its last addition at cycle $N - 1$ and it completes $L_a$ cycles later, so the total is $(N - 1) + L_a + \lceil \log_2 P \rceil L_a$. For $N = 270$, $L_a = 6$ and $P = 6$, that is $269 + 6 + 3 \times 6 = 293$ cycles, against $270 \times 6 = 1620$ for the original loop at II = 6. The extra cost is $P - 1$ registers and a short reduction, negligible for long loops. The same idea, splitting one long dependence chain into several shorter ones, is behind tree-height reduction in straight-line code.

## Going deeper

Kastner, Matai and Neuendorffer, "Parallel Programming for FPGAs" (2018), chapter on loop-carried dependences; Muchnick, "Advanced Compiler Design and Implementation" (1997), on reassociation.

lesson:
# Array partitioning: block, cyclic and complete

An array mapped to one RAM serves at most one or two accesses per cycle, which caps the II and the useful unroll factor of any loop that reads it. Array partitioning splits the array across several banks, each with its own ports. Choosing block, cyclic or complete partitioning, and the factor, is how an HLS designer matches memory bandwidth to the parallelism the schedule wants.

## Cyclic partitioning

Cyclic partitioning by a factor $B$ deals elements round-robin: element $i$ goes to bank $i \bmod B$ at offset $\lfloor i / B \rfloor$ inside it. With $B = 6$, element 50 lands in bank 2 at offset 8. Consecutive elements always fall in different banks, so a loop that reads $a[i], a[i+1], \dots, a[i+B-1]$ in one cycle touches every bank once. That makes cyclic partitioning the natural match for loops unrolled by a factor that divides or equals $B$ and that read neighbouring elements. Each bank is a smaller RAM, or a set of registers if it is small enough, and the address logic is cheap when $B$ is a power of two, because the modulo and division become bit selections. A non-power-of-two factor needs real modulo and division hardware on every access.

## Block partitioning

Block partitioning cuts the array into $B$ contiguous runs of $\lceil N / B \rceil$ elements: element $i$ goes to bank $\lfloor i / \lceil N / B \rceil \rfloor$ at offset $i \bmod \lceil N / B \rceil$. A 144-element array in 6 blocks has 24 elements per bank, so element 13 is in bank 0 and element 50 in bank 2. Neighbouring elements share a bank, so block partitioning does nothing for a loop that reads $a[i]$ and $a[i+1]$ together. It helps when parallel accesses are far apart: a loop that processes the two halves of an array simultaneously, or an outer loop unrolled so that each copy walks its own block. Complete partitioning, $B = N$, turns every element into its own register, which gives unlimited ports at the cost of $N$ registers and wide multiplexers on every access with a variable index.

## Choosing the factor

The factor should give exactly the bandwidth the schedule needs. If a loop is unrolled by U so that each cycle reads the U consecutive elements $a[Uk]$ through $a[Uk + U - 1]$, and each bank has $p$ ports, cyclic partitioning by $B$ spreads the U reads over $B$ banks, at most $\lceil U / B \rceil$ per bank. All reads fit in one cycle when $\lceil U / B \rceil \le p$, so the smallest factor is $B = \lceil U / p \rceil$: for U = 6 with dual-port banks, $B = 3$. A larger factor wastes RAM blocks, since each bank needs at least one physical block RAM however few elements it holds, while a smaller one raises the II. Multi-dimensional arrays can be partitioned along any dimension, and the right dimension is the one the unrolled loop index walks.

## Going deeper

Kastner, Matai and Neuendorffer, "Parallel Programming for FPGAs" (2018), chapter on arrays; Cong, Jiang, Liu and Zou, "Automatic memory partitioning and scheduling for throughput and power optimization" (ICCAD, 2009).

lesson:
# Bank conflicts and the II they force

Partitioning only helps if the accesses of one iteration spread over the banks. When two accesses in the same cycle hit the same bank, they conflict, and the schedule must spread them over extra cycles. Predicting bank conflicts from the access pattern is the computation an HLS memory partitioner performs, and it explains why a partitioned design can still miss its II.

## Which bank an access hits

With cyclic partitioning into $B$ banks, the access $a[i + o]$ touches bank $(i + o) \bmod B$. In the iteration with $i = 1$ and $B = 3$, the reads $a[i+1], a[i+2], a[i+3], a[i+4]$ and $a[i+8]$ touch elements 2, 3, 4, 5 and 9, which are in banks 2, 0, 1, 2 and 0. Two reads hit bank 2 and two hit bank 0. The pattern matters, not the absolute index: changing $i$ by one adds one to every bank number modulo $B$, which renames the banks but keeps the same grouping. So the conflict structure of a loop with constant offsets is determined by the offsets modulo $B$, and a partitioner can analyze it once, symbolically, for all iterations. For block partitioning the bank is the index divided by the bank size, and the pattern does change with $i$, which makes analysis harder.

## The busiest bank

Count the accesses per bank in one iteration and take the maximum. For offsets 0, 5, 6 and 7 with $B = 4$, the residues are 0, 1, 2 and 3, so every bank receives one access: a conflict-free pattern. For offsets 3, 4, 5 and 7 with $B = 2$, the residues are 1, 0, 1 and 1, so one bank receives three. The maximum per bank is the quantity that matters, because the busiest bank determines how many cycles the iteration's accesses need. A partitioner chooses $B$ to make the residues of the offsets as evenly spread as possible; for $k$ distinct consecutive offsets, $B \ge k$ guarantees one access per bank, but irregular offsets can conflict even with many banks, for example offsets 0 and 4 with $B = 4$.

## From conflicts to II

If the busiest bank receives $m$ accesses per iteration and each bank has $p$ ports, those accesses need $\lceil m / p \rceil$ cycles, and every iteration repeats them, so $\mathrm{II} \ge \lceil m / p \rceil$. Three accesses to one single-port bank force II = 3; with dual-port banks, II = 2. This is a ResMII bound in which each bank is its own resource. The fixes are a larger or different factor, a different partitioning dimension, or rewriting the code so that values are read once and passed through registers, as a shift register does for sliding windows. HLS reports phrase the result as an II violation on a memory port; the designer's job is to trace it back to the offsets and the bank function.

## Going deeper

Cong, Jiang, Liu and Zou, "Automatic memory partitioning and scheduling for throughput and power optimization" (ICCAD, 2009); Wang, Li and Cong, "Theory and algorithm for generalized memory partitioning in high-level synthesis" (FPGA, 2014).

lesson:
# Interface synthesis: handshakes, streams and buses

A synthesized kernel must exchange data with the rest of the system, and C function arguments say nothing about how. Interface synthesis maps each argument to a hardware protocol: a plain wire, a valid/ready handshake, a FIFO stream, a RAM port, or a memory-mapped bus master. The choice fixes bandwidth, sets II bounds and determines which verification problems can arise.

## Port-level protocols

The simplest interface is a plain port with no handshake: the block samples it whenever its schedule needs the value, so the environment must hold it stable. A valid signal adds timing: the producer raises valid when data is present. A full valid/ready handshake adds back-pressure: data transfers only on a clock edge where both valid and ready are high, and once a producer raises valid, it must keep the data and valid steady until the transfer happens. If the consumer drops ready for three cycles, the producer waits three cycles. Block-level control wraps the whole function call with start, done and idle signals, so a host can launch the accelerator and learn when it finishes. HLS tools generate these protocols from directives, and the protocol must match what the surrounding system actually does.

## Streams, memories and buses

An argument read once in order maps naturally to a stream, such as AXI4-Stream backed by a FIFO: no addresses, a handshake per item, and producer and consumer can overlap. An argument accessed randomly maps to a RAM interface with address, data and enable signals, limited to the RAM's ports. A large array in DRAM maps to a memory-mapped bus master, such as an AXI4 master port, which issues read and write transactions. Each transaction pays address and latency overhead, so the tool tries to infer bursts: one address phase followed by many data beats for consecutive addresses. Scalars and control usually go through a simple register interface such as AXI4-Lite, which a host processor writes and reads. The choice is made per argument and recorded in the generated RTL's ports.

## How interfaces bound performance

Interfaces are resources, and they bound the II. Two reads per iteration from a single-port RAM interface force II = 2. A DRAM read with 60 cycles of latency, issued one at a time with no bursts and no outstanding requests, limits a loop to roughly one element per 60 cycles, whatever its datapath II; bursts and multiple outstanding transactions hide that latency. Widening a bus helps only if each beat carries useful data: a 512-bit bus delivering 32-bit elements one per beat gives no gain, while packing 16 elements per beat gives up to 16 times the bandwidth. Streams add a different hazard: blocking FIFOs make depth part of correctness, since a producer that must write four items to a depth-2 FIFO before the consumer starts reading it will deadlock.

## Going deeper

The interface chapter of the AMD Vitis HLS user guide (UG1399); the AMBA AXI protocol specification from Arm; Kastner, Matai and Neuendorffer, "Parallel Programming for FPGAs" (2018).

lesson:
# Task-level dataflow

Loop pipelining overlaps iterations of one loop. Dataflow overlaps whole tasks: a function body made of several sub-functions or loops runs as a pipeline of processes connected by channels, so the second task works on frame $k$ while the first starts frame $k + 1$. It is how HLS builds streaming architectures, and its throughput is set by the slowest task, not the sum of all of them.

## Tasks, channels and the slowest stage

In a dataflow region each task is a process with its own controller, and tasks communicate through channels: FIFOs for streamed data, or ping-pong buffers, two memories that the producer and consumer swap between frames. A task's interval is how often it can accept a new frame; for a non-pipelined task it equals its latency, and for a pipelined task it can be smaller. In steady state the region accepts a new frame only as fast as its slowest task, so the interval between frames at the output is the maximum task interval. With tasks of intervals 240, 310 and 130 cycles, frames emerge every 310 cycles. Speeding up any task other than the slowest one does nothing for throughput; the designer, or a tool, must find and fix the bottleneck task.

## Total time for many frames

A simple model of a dataflow region charges the first frame the sum of the task latencies, since it must pass through every task, and every further frame the maximum interval. For $N$ frames the total is $\sum_t L_t + (N - 1)\max_t I_t$. With latencies 270, 580 and 410 and intervals 270, 170 and 410, 101 frames take $1260 + 100 \times 410 = 42260$ cycles. Sequential execution without dataflow would take $N \sum_t L_t = 101 \times 1260 = 127260$. The formula assumes channels never fill and tasks never wait on each other except for data; real regions can stall when a FIFO is too shallow for a burst, which the tool's co-simulation reveals. It is the same structure as loop pipelining, one level up: frames are iterations and tasks are stages.

## Speedup and the rules that make it possible

The speedup of dataflow over sequential execution is $\frac{N \sum L_t}{\sum L_t + (N - 1)\max I_t}$, which tends to $\sum L_t / \max I_t$ for many frames. With latencies summing to 700 and a maximum interval of 90, 49 frames give $34300 / 5020 = 6.83$, approaching 7.8. Dataflow requires discipline in the code: each channel must have a single producer and a single consumer, data must flow forward without feedback between tasks, and tasks must not share arrays except through channels. Violations make the tool fall back to sequential execution or insert conservative synchronization. Channel depth is a design parameter: ping-pong buffers double memory, and FIFOs must be deep enough to absorb rate mismatches, or the region deadlocks or stalls.

## Going deeper

The dataflow optimization chapter of the AMD Vitis HLS user guide (UG1399); Kastner, Matai and Neuendorffer, "Parallel Programming for FPGAs" (2018), chapter on streaming.

prereqs: Array partitioning: block, cyclic and complete
lesson:
# Line buffers and data reuse

Stencil computations, such as convolutions and filters over images, read each input many times. Fetching every window from external memory would need $K^2$ reads per output. Line buffers keep the most recent rows on chip, so each pixel is read from external memory once and reused from local storage. Sizing them is a small computation with large consequences for on-chip memory.

## How many pixels to keep

A $K \times K$ stencil over an image streamed in raster order, one pixel per cycle, needs the current pixel and the $K - 1$ rows above it. Keeping those rows on chip, $(K - 1) W$ pixels for an image of width $W$, lets each new pixel complete a window column with no external re-reads; the newest row streams in directly. A $5 \times 5$ convolution on a 2048-pixel-wide image keeps $4 \times 2048 = 8192$ pixels. A small window register of $K \times K$ pixels, shifted every cycle, holds the current window itself. External traffic drops from $K^2$ reads per output to one, which turns a bandwidth-bound kernel into a compute-bound one. The line buffers are an array accessed with a cyclic pattern, so each row is usually its own memory bank to give one read per row per cycle.

## Block RAMs for the buffers

Each buffered row is typically mapped to its own block RAM so that all $K - 1$ rows can be read in the same cycle. A row of $W$ pixels of $b$ bits needs $W b$ bits. Treating a block RAM as 18,432 bits of capacity, a row needs $\lceil W b / 18432 \rceil$ blocks, and the line buffers need $K - 1$ times that. A 3x3 stencil on 1024-pixel rows of 32-bit pixels needs $\lceil 32768 / 18432 \rceil = 2$ blocks per row, 4 in all. Real block RAMs come in fixed aspect ratios, so a narrow, deep row may waste capacity and the true count can be higher than this estimate. Wide pixels, wide images and large kernels multiply quickly, and line buffers can dominate the on-chip memory budget of an image pipeline.

## Latency to the first output

A line-buffered stencil cannot produce its first valid output until a full window is available. If pixel $(r, c)$ arrives in cycle $r W + c + 1$, the first window whose bottom-right pixel is $(K - 1, K - 1)$ is complete when that pixel arrives, in cycle $(K - 1) W + K$. For a $5 \times 5$ stencil on a 1024-wide image that is cycle 4101. This start-up latency is a fixed cost per frame, small relative to a full frame but important when frames are small or when the stencil sits inside a feedback loop. Border handling adds policy choices, such as padding, replicating edges or skipping invalid outputs, that change the output count and must match the reference model exactly, or co-simulation will flag differences at the image edges.

## Going deeper

Kastner, Matai and Neuendorffer, "Parallel Programming for FPGAs" (2018), chapter on image processing; Bailey, "Design for Embedded Image Processing on FPGAs" (2011).

lesson:
# Hardware-software partitioning

HLS is usually applied to part of a program: the kernel that dominates run time is moved to an accelerator while the rest stays in software. Deciding what to move, and whether the move pays once data transfer is counted, is hardware-software partitioning. Amdahl's law and a transfer-cost term give most of the answer before any synthesis is run.

## New run time after offloading

Let the software run time be $T$, the fraction spent in the candidate kernel $f$, the accelerator's speedup on that kernel $s$, and the added time for moving data to and from the accelerator $c$. The new run time is $T' = (1 - f) T + f T / s + c$. For $T = 440$ ms, $f = 0.7$, $s = 58$ and $c = 70.8$ ms, the software part stays at 132 ms, the kernel drops from 308 ms to 5.31 ms, and the transfer adds 70.8 ms, for 208.11 ms. Transfer often dominates: here it costs more than thirteen times the accelerated kernel itself. Overlapping transfer with computation, by streaming or double buffering, removes part of $c$, and keeping data resident on the accelerator across calls removes more.

## Overall speedup and Amdahl's limit

The overall speedup is $T / T'$. With $T = 780$ ms, $f = 0.83$, $s = 19$ and $c = 58.3$ ms, $T' = 132.6 + 34.07 + 58.3 = 224.97$ ms and the speedup is 3.47. However fast the accelerator, the speedup can never exceed $1 / (1 - f)$, here 5.88, because the software part remains. This is Amdahl's law, and it is the first filter in partitioning: a kernel covering 50% of run time can never give more than 2x overall. It also guides profiling: candidates should be ranked by the fraction of time they cover and by how much data they touch per unit of compute, since kernels with high arithmetic intensity amortize transfer best. A kernel that does little work per byte moved may need a speedup it can never reach.

## The break-even speedup

An accelerator pays off only if the kernel time it saves exceeds the transfer it adds: $f T / s + c < f T$, so $s > \frac{f T}{f T - c}$. For $T = 110$ ms, $f = 0.41$ and $c = 5$ ms, the kernel takes 45.1 ms in software, and the accelerator must run it at least $45.1 / 40.1 = 1.12$ times faster just to break even. If $c \ge f T$, no accelerator can help, because transfer alone costs more than the kernel. Partitioning tools formalize this as an optimization over many candidate kernels, with costs for area, transfer and synchronization, solved by ILP or heuristics; design-space exploration then tunes each chosen kernel. The same reasoning applies on-chip, between a processor and an accelerator sharing a cache.

## Going deeper

De Micheli and Gupta, "Hardware/software co-design" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 1997); Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach", the discussion of Amdahl's law.

# Design-space exploration of HLS directives

One C kernel admits thousands of microarchitectures through its directives: unroll factors, pipeline settings, partition factors, inlining, resource limits. Design-space exploration (DSE) searches that space for designs that trade latency against area well. The space is large, each evaluation costs a synthesis run, and the answer is a Pareto front rather than a single best point.

## The size of the directive space

Each directive choice multiplies the space. A kernel with three loops, each taking one of four unroll factors and pipelined or not, has $(4 \times 2)^3 = 512$ loop configurations; three arrays with three partitioning choices each multiply that by $3^3 = 27$, giving 13,824 points. With HLS runs taking minutes to hours, exhaustive search is out of reach even for small kernels. Many points are also illegal or pointless: a partition factor larger than the array, an unroll factor that exceeds the trip count, or a pipeline inside a fully unrolled loop. A practical explorer first prunes with cheap rules, then samples the remaining space, and spends synthesis runs only on configurations whose estimates look promising.

## Pareto-optimal designs

With two objectives to minimize, latency and area, a design dominates another when it is at least as good in both and strictly better in one. The Pareto front is the set of designs no other design dominates. Among (20 cycles, 1700 LUTs), (80, 900), (140, 1600), (40, 1100), (50, 1900), (100, 600) and (10, 1900), the design (140, 1600) is dominated by (80, 900), and (50, 1900) by (40, 1100), leaving five Pareto-optimal designs. A designer picks from the front according to the area budget or latency target; points off the front are never the right choice. Sorting by latency and sweeping while tracking the best area so far finds the front in $O(n \log n)$ for two objectives.

## Measuring a front with hypervolume

To compare explorers, measure the region a front dominates. The hypervolume indicator is the area of the set of points that are dominated by at least one front design and lie below a reference point $(L_{ref}, A_{ref})$. Sort the front by latency; between consecutive front latencies the dominated height is $A_{ref}$ minus the area of the earlier point. For a single front point (20, 100) and reference (220, 2200), the hypervolume is $200 \times 2100 = 420000$ cycle-LUTs. A larger hypervolume means a front that is closer to the ideal corner and better spread. Explorers based on Bayesian optimization or evolutionary search report hypervolume against the number of synthesis runs spent, which is the honest measure of exploration efficiency.

## Going deeper

Schafer and Wang, "High-level synthesis design space exploration: past, present, and future" (IEEE TCAD, 2020); Zitzler and Thiele, "Multiobjective evolutionary algorithms: a comparative case study and the strength Pareto approach" (IEEE TEC, 1999).

lesson:
# HLS tools and IRs: Vitis HLS, Bambu, CIRCT, Calyx

HLS is now built on compiler infrastructure. Commercial tools such as AMD Vitis HLS use LLVM-based front ends and expose the concepts of this domain as directives. Open tools and IRs, Bambu, CIRCT and its dialects, and the Calyx intermediate language, let a tool designer read and modify every stage. Knowing what each layer represents tells you where a new scheduling or binding idea should be implemented.

## Directives in a commercial flow

Vitis HLS exposes the main transformations as pragmas or directives. PIPELINE with an II target overlaps loop iterations. UNROLL replicates a loop body, fully or by a factor. ARRAY_PARTITION splits an array into banks, cyclic, block or complete, along a chosen dimension. DATAFLOW turns a function's sequence of sub-functions or loops into concurrent tasks connected by channels. INTERFACE chooses the protocol of each argument, such as a stream, an AXI4 master port or an AXI4-Lite register. INLINE controls whether a sub-function is merged into its caller. The report lists the achieved II per loop, its latency, resource estimates and the reason when a target II is missed. Every directive maps to a concept already covered here: modulo scheduling, unrolling, banking, dataflow and interface synthesis.

## Open tools and intermediate languages

Bambu, from the PandA project at Politecnico di Milano, is a complete open HLS framework: it takes C or C++ through a compiler front end and produces Verilog or VHDL, with its own scheduling, binding and memory allocation. CIRCT is an LLVM project that applies MLIR to hardware: a set of dialects at different abstraction levels, including handshake for dynamically scheduled dataflow circuits, Calyx for structured accelerators, and hw, comb and seq for RTL. Calyx, from Cornell, is an intermediate language whose components contain cells, groups of wire assignments, and a control program built from seq, par, if and while; its compiler turns the control program into finite-state machines. Lowering through several dialects lets each pass see the abstraction it needs.

## Static versus dynamic scheduling and MLIR-based HLS

Most HLS tools schedule statically: the compiler fixes every operation's cycle, and the controller is an FSM. Dynamically scheduled HLS, as in the Dynamatic tool and CIRCT's handshake dialect, builds elastic circuits in which each operation fires when its input tokens arrive through valid/ready channels. A loop whose branch arms take 2 or 20 cycles runs at the speed of the path actually taken, where a static schedule must budget for the slow arm; the price is handshake logic and buffers on every channel. MLIR-based flows such as ScaleHLS perform loop transformations in the affine dialect, where loop bounds and indices are affine functions so dependence analysis is exact, and then emit HLS C++ with directives. LLVM IR alone loses much of the loop and array structure these transformations need.

## Going deeper

label: Seams and change tiers in an HLS engine
lesson:
# Seams and change tiers in an HLS engine

An HLS engine built for agents separates what must never change casually, the rules that make every schedule and binding correct, from what customers and agents tune: priorities, cost functions, directive values and observation points. Applying the four-layer engine model and the change tiers to HLS tells a tool designer where each kind of request lands and what proof it needs before it ships.

## The four layers of an HLS engine

The immutable core holds correctness: dependence analysis, including loop-carried and memory dependences, the precedence and modulo reservation checks, and the rule that every binding is a proper coloring of its conflict graph. Changing it needs human approval and full regression. The strategy layer holds policies that choose among legal results: list-scheduling priorities, force-directed or SDC objectives, binding cost functions that weigh multiplexers against units. The parameter layer holds values: target clock, II targets, unroll and partition factors, resource limits, all changeable without recompiling. The observation layer exposes live state: per-loop achieved II, the limiting resource or recurrence, the chosen schedule, register and multiplexer counts. A request to log each scheduling decision is a hook; a request to favour store-feeding operations is policy; raising an unroll cap is a parameter.

## Which tier a request lands in

Requests are handled at the smallest safe tier. Pipelining every loop at II = 2 with unrolling capped at 4 is Tier 1: directive and parameter values the engine already reads. A binding cost that penalizes sharing a multiplier between operands from different memory banks is Tier 2: new behavior, but it only re-ranks legal bindings, so it belongs at the binder's cost-function seam. Letting the scheduler ignore a loop-carried memory dependence to reach a lower II is Tier 3, if it is allowed at all, because it changes what function the hardware computes. Customer-specific operator latencies belong behind an operator-characterization interface that the scheduler, chaining and binder query per operation, width and target, so that a new device or library becomes a Tier 1 table or a Tier 2 provider, never a core edit.

## Designing the seams and proving changes

A good seam is narrow and stable: an abstract interface with a factory, called coarsely, per batch of operations or per loop rather than once per operation inside the binder's innermost loop, so the hot kernel stays inlinable. Plug-ins receive plain data, keep no hidden global state and are deterministic and seedable; a plug-in that reads state left over from a previous run makes differential tests irreproducible. Every change is proven against a golden kernel suite: all kernels still pass C/RTL co-simulation, and a QoR differential report shows that latency, II, registers and area moved only where the change intended. A new priority that shortens one kernel and silently lengthens three others fails that review, even though every output is still correct.

## Going deeper

For the engine model, the agent_first_eda lessons on the four-layer model, change tiers and seams; for HLS internals, Coussy and Morawiec (eds.), "High-Level Synthesis: From Algorithm to Digital Circuit" (2008).

lesson:
# Pragma-search agents

Choosing HLS directives is a search over a huge discrete space with an expensive, noisy evaluator, exactly the kind of loop an agent can run. A pragma-search agent proposes directive settings, runs HLS, reads the report and decides the next experiment. Done well, it reaches good Pareto points in far fewer runs than blind search; done badly, it games estimates and ships unverified designs.

## The search problem

The directive space multiplies: a few loops and arrays with a handful of options each give thousands of configurations, and each HLS run takes minutes to hours. An agent therefore works at Tier 1: it edits directive values such as II targets, unroll factors and partition factors, never the engine. Before spending a run it applies cheap legality and resource checks: complete partitioning of a million-element array would need a million registers and can be rejected immediately, and an unroll factor beyond the trip count is equivalent to full unrolling. After each run it reads the structured report, the achieved II and latency per loop, resource use, and the stated reason a loop missed its target, rather than only a pass or fail code. The report is the observation hook the agent's decisions depend on.

## Reading the report to choose the next move

The most valuable information in an HLS report is the binding constraint. A loop at II = 4 limited by the memory ports of array A calls for partitioning A cyclically or restructuring its accesses; adding multipliers would change nothing. A loop at II = 5 limited by a carried dependence through $s$ is RecMII-bound: partitioning arrays will not lower it, and the fix is to reassociate or break the recurrence, which is a source change outside the agent's Tier 1 remit and must go to a human or a reviewed transformation. Each proposal is judged as a delta against a stored baseline for that kernel. When two proposals give identical reports, the varied directives did not touch the binding constraint, and a good policy moves its search elsewhere instead of repeating similar points.

## Rewards, proxies and verification

An agent rewarded only on reported latency learns to unroll and partition everything, spending unlimited area; the objective must include resource limits or be posed as a Pareto search. HLS reports are estimates that miss routing delay and congestion, so a design with excellent reported numbers may miss timing after implementation; the loop must recurse into the accurate engines, logic synthesis and place and route, for the finalists. A result that never ran C/RTL co-simulation is unverified, however good its QoR, since directives like dataflow or interface changes can introduce protocol or ordering bugs. And some moves must stay out of the agent's hands entirely: editing the C source to delete a dependence the agent judges unnecessary can change the function computed, and needs human review.

## Going deeper

Schafer and Wang, "High-level synthesis design space exploration: past, present, and future" (IEEE TCAD, 2020); the agent_first_eda lessons on the harness loop and fast versus accurate engines.

lesson:
# LLM-to-HLS-C translation loops

Language models can translate a reference algorithm, written in Python, MATLAB or plain C, into synthesizable HLS-C with directives. The output is only useful inside a harness that compiles it, simulates it against the reference, synthesizes it and co-simulates the RTL, feeding each failure back to the model. Designing that loop, and knowing what each stage can and cannot catch, is the engineering problem.

## What makes generated code synthesizable

HLS accepts a subset of C and C++. Models trained mostly on software code readily produce constructs outside it: growing containers such as a vector with push_back, which have no static hardware size; recursion of data-dependent depth, which needs an unbounded stack; unbounded while-loops, which synthesize but have unknown worst-case latency and need an explicit trip-count bound; pointers whose aliasing the tool cannot resolve. Fixed-size arrays, bounded for-loops, streams and arbitrary-precision integer types are the safe vocabulary. The cheapest first check is to compile the code and run the C testbench against the reference outputs, which takes seconds and catches functional errors before any synthesis time is spent. A harness that front-loads cheap checks keeps the expensive tools for candidates that can actually succeed.

## The harness loop

The loop orders its checks by cost: C compile, C simulation, HLS synthesis, then C/RTL co-simulation, each requiring the previous one to pass. On a failure, the harness returns specific feedback: the compiler or HLS error message with the offending source lines, the first mismatching output vector, or the report's II violation reason and the loop it names. A C pass is not enough to accept the code. The C may rely on behavior the hardware does not reproduce, such as reading uninitialized memory or depending on overflow, and co-simulation is where those mismatches appear. When synthesis succeeds but misses its target, for example II = 8 instead of 1, the next prompt should carry the reported limiting resource or recurrence, so the model can restructure the loop instead of guessing.

## Measuring and bounding the system

The right metric is tool-grounded: the fraction of tasks whose output passes C simulation and co-simulation, together with QoR against a baseline implementation; text similarity to a human kernel rewards code that looks right rather than code that works. Tests must cover boundaries: a model that removes a bounds check never triggered by the testbench passes every test, so coverage of edge cases and randomized vectors is the defense. Number formats matter: replacing a 16-bit fixed-point reference with float changes both the results and the area, and the acceptance tolerance must come from the specification. When an external API model drives the loop, the IP-boundary principle applies: decide explicitly what design data may leave the site, and keep tools, vectors and results inside the sandbox.

## Going deeper

The agent_first_eda lessons on the harness loop, golden testing and sandboxing; Kastner, Matai and Neuendorffer, "Parallel Programming for FPGAs" (2018), on writing synthesizable HLS code.

lesson:
# Co-simulation as the golden test

In an HLS flow the C model is the specification, and C/RTL co-simulation is the test that checks the generated hardware against it. For agent-driven flows, whether an agent writes the C, tunes the directives or edits the engine itself, co-simulation is the golden check and the most trustworthy reward signal. Knowing what it proves, and what it cannot, is essential before trusting any automated result.

## What co-simulation checks

Co-simulation runs the original C testbench twice: once calling the C function, and once driving the generated RTL through adapters that translate arguments into the RTL's interface protocols, and it compares the outputs. Because the C model is what the RTL was generated from, and it runs fast enough to label many vectors, it is the golden reference. A pass shows that on the tested vectors the outputs match, the handshakes complete and the RTL terminates. It also measures what the HLS report only estimates: the actual latency and interval in cycles on those inputs, including stalls and variable-latency loops. It does not show that the design meets timing after implementation, nor that it is correct on untested inputs; those need static timing analysis and better coverage.

## Golden and differential tests for engine changes

When the HLS engine itself changes, a golden kernel suite with known-good outputs guards it. A good suite exercises distinct features: recurrences, partitioned arrays, streams, branches, dataflow regions, multicycle operators. For a new scheduling heuristic the differential test is: every kernel still passes co-simulation, and the QoR differences in latency, II, registers and area are the intended ones. Byte-identical RTL is the wrong criterion there, because a scheduler change should change schedules; it is the right criterion for a behavior-preserving refactor, such as restructuring the RTL emitter, where any difference is a regression. A binding change that keeps all co-simulations passing but raises area by 9% on two kernels must still be flagged: golden tests guard correctness, the QoR baseline guards quality.

## Where the golden test is weak

A golden test is only as strong as its stimulus. A testbench that never stalls a stream output never exercises the hold-while-not-ready path, so back-pressure bugs slip through; the test must randomize ready and valid. Ten hand-picked vectors miss corner cases that randomized and coverage-directed vectors, labelled by the C model, catch. Floating-point comparison needs care: a permitted reassociation changes rounding, so the comparison must use a tolerance justified by the numerical specification, while integer paths stay bit-exact. For learned generators, co-simulation is the right reward: a reward based only on the HLS report's latency can be maximized by code that computes the wrong function, which is reward hacking, while a co-simulation-gated reward grounds the score in correct behavior.

## Going deeper

The C/RTL co-simulation chapter of the AMD Vitis HLS user guide (UG1399); the agent_first_eda lessons on golden and differential testing and on tool-grounded reinforcement learning.

# Fast QoR surrogates for exploration

Every HLS run costs minutes; every implementation run costs far more. Design-space explorers therefore use surrogate models that predict latency, II and resources from a configuration in milliseconds, and spend real runs only on promising points. A surrogate is the fast engine in a fast-accurate loop, and it must be judged by how well it supports the decisions it drives, not only by its average error.

## Error of a single prediction

A surrogate maps a kernel and directive configuration to predicted QoR: from analytical models built on the schedule's bounds, such as $(N - 1)\,\mathrm{II} + L$ with ResMII and RecMII estimates, from learned models over features of the CDFG and directives, or from graph neural networks over the IR. For one configuration, the absolute percentage error is $|p - a| / a \times 100$, comparing prediction $p$ with the value $a$ from full synthesis. A prediction of 3520 cycles against an actual 4250 has an error of 17.2%. Analytical estimates are often exact for latency when the schedule is regular and badly off when the true binding constraint is something the model ignores, such as a memory port or a carried dependence through memory. Resource predictions are harder, because binding and logic optimization change them a lot.

## Mean absolute percentage error

Averaging the percentage errors over a validation set gives the mean absolute percentage error, $\mathrm{MAPE} = \frac{100}{n} \sum_i |p_i - a_i| / a_i$. For four designs with errors of 5.4%, 13.7%, 18.6% and 5.0%, MAPE is 10.7%. MAPE is scale-free, so a 50-cycle error on a 100-cycle design weighs more than on a 10,000-cycle one, which suits latency that spans orders of magnitude. The validation set must come from configurations the surrogate did not train on, ideally from kernels it has never seen, or the error estimate will be optimistic. A surrogate with a low MAPE on one kernel family can fail on another, which is why an explorer must periodically check it against real runs and fall back to the accurate engine when it drifts.

## Ranking quality matters more than error

An explorer uses a surrogate to choose which configurations to synthesize, so what matters is whether it orders candidates correctly. Count the discordant pairs: pairs of designs that the surrogate orders differently from full synthesis. Among five designs there are 10 pairs, and Kendall's $\tau$ is $(\text{concordant} - \text{discordant}) / 10$. A surrogate with a large constant bias has a high MAPE but can rank perfectly; one with small errors near the Pareto front can rank badly exactly where decisions are made. So explorers measure rank correlation near the front, synthesize the top candidates rather than trusting the single predicted best, and recurse into the accurate engine whenever the surrogate's ranking of candidates disagrees with the real results.

## Going deeper

Schafer and Wang, "High-level synthesis design space exploration: past, present, and future" (IEEE TCAD, 2020); the agent_first_eda lesson on fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop.
